components.note: 言 (speech) — 譬 involves explaining something through words.
辟 (pì) gives the sound — an exact match with 譬.

example.english: For example, apples are fruit.
example.fact: 譬 is mostly seen in 譬如 (pìrú), a formal way to say "for example."

components.note: 文 (culture, writing) — 斌 describes someone refined, accomplished in both culture and martial skill.

example.english: His name is Bin.
example.fact: 斌 combines 文 (culture) and 武 (military), symbolizing being well-rounded — a popular character in Chinese given names.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, ritual) — 祈 concerns communicating with the spirits or gods.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound distantly related to qí, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: They are praying for peace.
example.fact: 祈 mainly appears in 祈祷 (qídǎo, "to pray") and 祈求 (qíqiú, "to beseech").

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踢 is an action done with the foot.
易 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to tī, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: We like playing soccer.
example.fact: 踢足球 (tī zúqiú, "to play soccer") is one of the most common phrases using 踢.

etymologyHint: Having long 镸 hair 聿

components.note: 镸 depicts something long or elongated.

聿 depicts a hand holding a brush — together with 镸, an old picture of long, flowing hair, from which 肆's meaning 'excess, indulgence' later developed. Today 肆 is mostly known as the formal, complex form of the numeral 'four.'

example.hanzi: 写支票时,数字四要写成肆。
example.pinyin: Xiě zhīpiào shí, shùzì sì yào xiě chéng sì.
example.english: When writing a check, the number four should be written as 肆.
example.fact: In formal documents like checks, simple numerals such as 四 (four) are replaced with complex characters like 肆 to prevent forgery.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坎 describes a pit or raised edge in the ground.
欠 (qiàn) gives a sound distantly related to kǎn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: There's a step at the doorway, be careful.
example.fact: 坎 commonly appears in 门坎 (ménkǎn, "doorsill, threshold").

etymologyHint: A lofty 乔 carriage 车; 乔 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 车 (a vehicle) — 轿 refers to a carried vehicle, a sedan chair.
乔 depicts something tall or lofty, describing the raised seat of a sedan chair.

example.english: In ancient times, brides rode in a sedan chair to their wedding.
example.fact: 轿子 (jiàozi) were carried by two or more people and were a common way for the wealthy to travel before cars existed.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 棚 is a structure typically built from wood or bamboo.
朋 (péng) gives the sound — an exact match with 棚.

example.english: There's a shed in the garden.
example.fact: 棚子 (péngzi) refers to a simple shed or awning, often built from wood or bamboo.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泣 relates to tears.
立 (lì) gives a sound distantly related to qì, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: She cried softly.
example.fact: 泣 is a more literary word for crying, often paired with 哭 as 哭泣 (kūqì).

components.note: 尸 (body) — used here as a general classifier-like radical, unrelated in meaning to 屡's modern sense.
娄 (lóu) gives a sound distantly related to lǚ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He is late time and again.
example.fact: 屡 almost always appears in the two-character word 屡次 (lǚcì, "time and again").

components.note: 足 (foot) — originally linked to restless movement, like stamping one's feet impatiently.
喿 (zào) gives the sound — an exact match with 躁.

example.english: Don't be agitated, take it slowly.
example.fact: 躁 usually appears in 急躁 (jízào, "impatient") or 烦躁 (fánzào, "agitated").

etymologyHint: A place 阝 on a hill 丘; 丘 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 阝, here representing a settlement, sits beside the hill.
丘 depicts a small hill or mound; 邱 was originally a place name and is mostly seen today as a surname.

example.english: My friend's surname is Qiu.
example.fact: 邱 is a common Chinese surname and originated as a variant of 丘 (hill), a place-name element.

meanings: used in 鳳凰|凤凰[feng4 huang2]

components.note: 几, shown here as an enclosing shape, forms the outer frame of the character.
皇 (huáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 凰.

example.pinyin: Fènghuáng shì chuánshuō zhōng de niǎo.
example.english: The phoenix is a legendary bird.
example.fact: 凰 almost never appears alone — it is always paired with 凤 (fèng) to form 凤凰 (fènghuáng), the mythical Chinese phoenix.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 溢 describes liquid spilling over.
益 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 溢.

example.pinyin: Shuǐ tài duō, yì chūlái le.
example.english: There's too much water, it overflowed.
example.fact: 溢 commonly appears in 溢出 (yìchū, "to overflow") describing liquid spilling over an edge.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 椎 originally named a wooden mallet or hammer.
隹 (zhuī) gives a sound close to chuí, having drifted apart slightly over time.

example.english: The spine is very important for the body.
example.fact: Though 椎 originally meant a wooden mallet, its most common modern use is in 脊椎 (jǐzhuī, "spine, vertebra").

components.note: 石 (rock) — 砸 involves a hard, crushing impact.
匝 (zā) gives a sound close to zá, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā bù xiǎoxīn bǎ bēizi zá le.
example.english: He accidentally smashed the cup.
example.fact: 砸 is the everyday word for breaking something by dropping or striking it hard.

components.note: 走 (walk) — 趟 describes making a trip on foot or in general.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound distantly related to tàng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I made a trip to the supermarket.
example.fact: 趟 is a measure word for a single round trip or journey, as in 去一趟 (qù yí tàng, "to make a trip").

meanings: flag used as a shop sign
etymologyHint: A curtain 巾 at the entrance to a cave 穴

components.note: 穴 depicts a cave or hole, here representing an entrance or opening.
巾 (cloth) hangs at the entrance, forming the picture of a curtain covering an opening.

example.english: Please open the curtain.
example.fact: 帘 is most often seen in 窗帘 (chuānglián, "window curtain"), a common household word.

meanings: Taiwan pr. [fan2], except 帆布[fan1 bu4] canvas

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 帆 is a piece of cloth used to catch wind.
凡 (fán) gives a sound close to fān, differing only in tone.

example.english: There is a sailboat on the sea.
example.fact: 帆 refers to the cloth sail itself, most often seen in 帆船 (fānchuán, "sailboat").

components.note: 木 (tree) — 栖 describes resting or roosting, often in a tree.
西 (xī) gives a sound close to qī, sharing the same final.

example.pinyin: Xiǎo niǎo xǐhuan qīxī zài shù shàng.
example.english: Little birds like to perch in trees.
example.fact: 栖 mostly appears in 栖息 (qīxī), meaning for an animal to rest or live somewhere, especially birds in trees.

etymologyHint: Simplified form of 竄; a mouse 鼠 running out of its hole 穴

components.note: 穴 (a hole, cave) — 窜 originally depicted a rodent's burrow.
串, resembling a running shape here, replaced the original 鼠 (mouse) component when the character was simplified — together giving 窜 its meaning 'to flee, to scurry away.'

example.pinyin: Lǎoshǔ cuàn jìn le dòng lǐ.
example.english: The mouse scurried into the hole.
example.fact: 窜 vividly describes fleeing or bolting away suddenly, as in 逃窜 (táocuàn, "to flee in a panic").

etymologyHint: A fist 九 holding a pebble 丶

components.note: 九, used here purely for its curled shape rather than its meaning 'nine,' pictures a hand or fist.
丶 represents a small round object, like a pebble or pill, held within the fist.

example.english: Mom made fish balls.
example.fact: 丸 describes anything small and round, from medicine pills to food like 鱼丸 (yúwán, "fish balls").

meanings: to behead (as form of capital punishment)

components.note: 斤 (axe) — 斩 describes cutting with a blade.
车 (chē) gives a sound distantly related to zhǎn, having drifted far apart over time.

example.english: In ancient times, criminals could be beheaded.
example.fact: 斩 is a formal, mostly literary/historical word for cutting or beheading, as in 斩首 (zhǎnshǒu).

components.note: 土 (earth) — 堤 is a raised bank of earth.
是 (shì) gives a sound distantly related to dī, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The river dike protects the city.
example.fact: 堤 refers to an embankment built to hold back water, as in 河堤 (hédī, "river dike").

components.note: 土 (earth) — 塌 describes something, like a building or roof, sinking or collapsing to the ground.

example.english: The old house collapsed.
example.fact: 塌 describes a structure caving in, as in 倒塌 (dǎotā, "to collapse").

components.note: 贝 (money) — 贩 relates to trading for profit.
反 (fǎn) gives a sound close to fàn, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Jiē shàng yǒu hěn duō xiǎofàn.
example.english: There are many street vendors on the street.
example.fact: 贩 refers to buying and selling goods for profit, most often in 小贩 (xiǎofàn, "street peddler").

components.note: 厂 (building) — 厢 refers to a room or compartment attached to a main structure.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 厢.

example.pinyin: Huǒchē chēxiāng lǐ rén hěn duō.
example.english: There are many people in the train carriage.
example.fact: 厢 today is mostly used in 车厢 (chēxiāng), the compartment or carriage of a train.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掀 is an action done by hand.
欣 (xīn) gives a sound close to xiān, sharing the same initial.

example.english: He flipped the book open.
example.fact: 掀 describes lifting something like a lid or cover, as in 掀开 (xiān kāi, "to lift open").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喀 is used for sounds made with the mouth or by an object.
客 (kè) gives a sound close to kā, sharing the same initial.

example.pinyin: Shùzhī kāchā yì shēng duàn le.
example.english: The branch snapped with a cracking sound.
example.fact: 喀 is mainly used for sound effects, like 喀嚓 (kāchā, the crack/snap sound), or in place names such as 喀什 (Kāshí).

example.english: This child is very well-behaved.
example.fact: 乖 is what Chinese parents say to praise a well-behaved child, often as 你真乖 (nǐ zhēn guāi, "you're so good").

meanings: see 謎兒|谜儿[mei4 r5], riddle
etymologyHint: Bewitching 迷 words 讠; 迷 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谜 is something expressed in words that puzzles the listener.
迷 pictures being lost or bewildered; combined with speech 讠, this gives 谜 its meaning 'a riddle' — words designed to confuse.

example.english: Guessing riddles is fun.
example.fact: 谜 is the character for a riddle or puzzle, as in 谜语 (míyǔ, "riddle").

meanings: to hold between the thumb and fingers

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捏 is an action done with the fingers.
圼 (niè) gives a sound close to niē; 圼 is a rare character used mainly as a phonetic here.

example.pinyin: Tā niē le yí gè miànrén.
example.english: She molded a dough figure by hand.
example.fact: 捏 refers to shaping something with the fingers, as in 捏面人 (niē miànrén, "to sculpt dough figures"), a traditional Chinese folk art.

components.note: 门 (gate) — 阎 originally referred to a village or lane gate.
臽 (xiàn) gives a sound distantly related to yán, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: His surname is Yan.
example.fact: 阎 is best known today as a surname, and appears in 阎王 (Yánwáng), the King of Hell in Chinese folklore.

meanings: (bound form) to border on (a lake, river etc)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 滨 describes the edge of a body of water.
宾 (bīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 滨.

example.english: We took a walk by the seaside.
example.fact: 滨 usually appears in 海滨 (hǎibīn, "seaside") or city names like 哈尔滨 (Hā'ěrbīn, Harbin).

components.note: 力 (strength) — 虏 originally related to subduing someone by force.
虍 (hū) gives a sound distantly related to lǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The soldiers captured prisoners.
example.fact: 虏 almost always appears in 俘虏 (fúlǔ), meaning a prisoner of war.

meanings: used in 鑰匙|钥匙[yao4 shi5]

components.note: 匕 (a blade-like shape, used for spoon-like utensils) — 匙 named a spoon.
是 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with the "shi" reading of 匙.

example.english: I forgot to bring my keys.
example.fact: Though 匙 alone can mean "spoon" (chí), it's most commonly seen today in 钥匙 (yàoshi, "key"), where it's pronounced with a neutral tone "shi."

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 芦 names a type of tall grass.
户 (hù) gives a sound distantly related to lú, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Reeds grow by the riverside.
example.fact: 芦 mostly appears in 芦苇 (lúwěi, "reed"), a tall grass common near water.

meanings: used in 蘋果|苹果[ping2 guo3]

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 苹 names a fruiting plant.
平 (píng) gives the sound — an exact match with 苹.

example.english: I like eating apples.
example.fact: 苹 never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it's always part of 苹果 (píngguǒ, "apple").

meanings: to unload; to remove; to detach; to get rid of

components.note: 止 (stop) — 卸 describes bringing something to a halt and removing it.
卩 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to xiè, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The workers are unloading cargo.
example.fact: 卸 describes removing or taking something off, as in 卸货 (xièhuò, "unload goods") or 卸妆 (xièzhuāng, "remove makeup").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沼 names a body of standing water.
召 (zhào) gives a sound close to zhǎo, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Zhǎozé lǐ yǒu hěn duō dòngwù.
example.english: There are many animals in the swamp.
example.fact: 沼 is mostly seen in 沼泽 (zhǎozé, "swamp, marsh").

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钥 names an object made of metal.
月 (yuè) gives a sound distantly related to yào, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: What should I do if I lost my key?
example.fact: 钥 almost never stands alone — it pairs with 匙 to form 钥匙 (yàoshi, "key"), reflecting that keys were traditionally made of metal.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 株 names or counts trees.
朱 (zhū) gives the sound — an exact match with 株.

example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ zhòng le yì zhū shù.
example.english: A tree was planted in the yard.
example.fact: 株 is a measure word for plants and trees, as in 一株树 (yì zhū shù, "one tree").

components.note: 礻 (spirit) — 祷 concerns communicating with the spirits or gods.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound distantly related to dǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: They are praying in the church.
example.fact: 祷 usually appears with 祈 in 祈祷 (qídǎo, "to pray").

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剖 involves cutting something open.
咅 (pǒu) gives a sound close to pōu, differing only in tone.

example.english: The doctor is dissecting a frog.
example.fact: 剖 means to cut open for examination, as in 解剖 (jiěpōu, "to dissect") or 剖腹产 (pōufùchǎn, "cesarean section").

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 熙 relates to brightness and warmth.
巸 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 熙.

example.hanzi: 康熙是一位有名的皇帝。
example.pinyin: Kāngxī shì yí wèi yǒumíng de huángdì.
example.english: Kangxi was a famous emperor.
example.fact: 熙 is best known from 康熙 (Kāngxī), the reign name of a famous Qing dynasty emperor, and is common in given names for its meaning "bright, flourishing."

meanings: sound of gurgling, splashing or flowing water

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哗 is used for sounds.
华 (huá) gives a sound close to huā, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Huālā yì shēng, yǔ xià dà le.
example.english: With a rushing sound, the rain poured down.
example.fact: 哗 is an onomatopoeic character imitating the sound of rushing water or a loud noise, as in 哗啦 (huālā).

components.note: 刀 (knife) — 劈 involves cutting with a blade.
辟 (pì) gives a sound close to pī, sharing the same initial and final.

example.english: He split open the wood.
example.fact: 劈 describes a chopping motion with a sharp blade, as in 劈开 (pī kāi, "to split open").

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怯 describes an inner state of fear.
去 (qù) gives a sound distantly related to qiè, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He's a bit timid.
example.fact: 怯 usually appears in 胆怯 (dǎnqiè, "cowardly, timid").

components.note: 木 (tree) — 棠 names a type of tree.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound distantly related to táng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Begonia flowers are very pretty.
example.fact: 棠 is mostly seen in 海棠 (hǎitáng), a flowering crab-apple tree popular in Chinese gardens.

meanings: used in 胳肢窩|胳肢窝[ga1 zhi5 wo1]

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 胳 names a body part.
各 (gè) gives a sound close to gē, sharing the same initial.

example.english: My arm hurts a lot.
example.fact: 胳 never stands alone — it's always part of 胳膊 (gēbo, "arm").

components.note: 木 (wood) — 桩 originally named a wooden stake or post.
庄 (zhuāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 桩.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì zhuāng zhòngyào de shì.
example.english: This is an important matter.
example.fact: Besides meaning a wooden stake, 桩 is also a measure word for events or affairs, as in 一桩事 (yì zhuāng shì).

components.note: 王 (jade) — 瑰 originally described a fine, precious stone.
鬼 (guǐ) gives a sound close to guī, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā sòng le tā yì duǒ méiguī huā.
example.english: He gave her a rose.
example.fact: 瑰 is mostly seen in 玫瑰 (méiguī, "rose"), the flower name.

components.note: 女 (woman) — an older semantic link to leisure and enjoyment.
吴 (wú) gives a sound close to yú, sharing the same final.

example.pinyin: Kàn diànyǐng shì yì zhǒng yúlè.
example.english: Watching movies is a form of entertainment.
example.fact: 娱 is almost always seen in 娱乐 (yúlè, "entertainment").

etymologyHint: To take 取 a wife 女; 取 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 取 means 'to take, to obtain' — pictured here on top.
女 (woman) sits below — together with 取, the image is of 'taking a woman [as a wife],' giving 娶 its meaning 'to marry (a woman).'

example.english: He married her last year.
example.fact: 娶 specifically means for a man to take a wife, contrasting with 嫁 (jià), which describes a woman marrying into a family.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沫 names bubbles on the surface of a liquid.
末 (mò) gives the sound — an exact match with 沫.

example.english: Soap can produce foam.
example.fact: 沫 usually appears in 泡沫 (pàomò, "foam, bubbles").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗓 names a part of the mouth/throat used for speaking.
桑 (sāng) gives a sound close to sǎng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 我嗓子疼,不能大声说话。
example.pinyin: Wǒ sǎngzi téng, bù néng dàshēng shuōhuà.
example.english: My throat hurts, I can't speak loudly.
example.fact: 嗓 usually appears in 嗓子 (sǎngzi), referring to the throat or one's voice.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹲 describes a posture involving the legs and feet.
尊 (zūn) gives a sound distantly related to dūn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā dūn zài dìshàng kàn shū.
example.english: He squatted on the ground reading.
example.fact: 蹲 describes lowering your body by bending your knees while keeping your feet flat — a common resting position in China.

etymologyHint: Setting fire 火 to a forest 林

components.note: 林 (two trees together) pictures a forest or grove.
火 (fire) is set beneath the forest 林 — a vivid picture giving 焚 its meaning 'to burn.'

example.english: They are burning trash.
example.fact: 焚 is a literary word for burning, as in the idiom 玩火自焚 (wánhuǒ zìfén, "to play with fire and get burned").

meanings: to dredge; to scoop out (sediment or waste)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淘 originally described washing something in water.
匋 (táo) gives the sound — an exact match with 淘.

example.english: This child is very naughty.
example.fact: 淘 originally meant washing something in water (like rice or sand), but 淘气 (táoqì) today just means "naughty, mischievous."

components.note: 女 (woman) — an older semantic link to softness and youth.
敕 (chì) gives a sound distantly related to nèn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This piece of meat is very tender.
example.fact: 嫩 describes something soft, tender, or young — used for food, plants, or young skin and leaves.

etymologyHint: Of equal 匀 tone 音; 匀 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 音 (sound) forms the left side — 韵 concerns qualities of sound.
匀 means 'even, uniform' — paired with sound 音, the image is of evenly balanced tones, giving 韵 its meaning 'rhyme, tonal charm.'

example.english: This poem rhymes well.
example.fact: 韵 refers to rhyme or tonal harmony in poetry and music, as in 押韵 (yāyùn, "to rhyme").

components.note: 衤 (clothes) — 衬 names an item of clothing.
寸 (cùn) gives a sound distantly related to chèn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā chuān le yí jiàn bái chènshān.
example.english: He wore a white shirt.
example.fact: 衬 is most familiar from 衬衫 (chènshān, "shirt"), one of the first clothing words learners encounter.

meanings: abbr. for 匈牙利[Xiong1 ya2 li4]

components.note: 勹 (wrap) — an old semantic link to an enclosed or bound shape.
凶 (xiōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 匈.

example.hanzi: 匈牙利是一个欧洲国家。
example.pinyin: Xiōngyálì shì yí gè Ōuzhōu guójiā.
example.english: Hungary is a European country.
example.fact: 匈 today mainly appears in 匈牙利 (Xiōngyálì, "Hungary") and historically referred to the Xiongnu (匈奴) nomadic people.

meanings: unit of measure equivalent to thirty catties

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钧 originally referred to a unit of weight for metal.
匀 (yún) gives a sound distantly related to jūn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: One "jun" equals thirty jin (catties).
example.fact: 钧 was an ancient unit of weight equal to thirty catties (斤), and is also used as a respectful term of address in formal letters.

etymologyHint: A person 又 standing 立 as straight as a knife 刂

components.note: 刂 (a knife blade) suggests something straight and sharp.
又 here represents a person's hand or figure.
立 (to stand) sits below — together, the image is of a person standing as straight as a blade, giving 竖 its meaning 'vertical, upright.'

example.english: Please write a vertical stroke.
example.fact: 竖 names the basic vertical stroke (丨) used in writing Chinese characters, and more generally means "vertical, upright."

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峻 describes the height and steepness of terrain.
夋 (qūn) gives a sound distantly related to jùn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This mountain is very steep.
example.fact: 峻 describes something high and steep, as in 险峻 (xiǎnjùn, "precipitous") often describing mountains.

components.note: 豸 (beast) — 豹 names an animal.
勺 (sháo) gives a sound distantly related to bào, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Leopards run very fast.
example.fact: 豹 refers to leopards and panthers, animals known for their speed and spotted coats.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 捞 is an action done by hand.
劳 (láo) gives a sound close to lāo, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Tā cóng shuǐ lǐ lāo chū yì tiáo yú.
example.english: He scooped a fish out of the water.
example.fact: 捞 describes fishing or scooping something out of water or liquid by hand or net.

components.note: 艹 (flower, grass) — 菊 names a flowering plant.
匊 (jú) gives the sound — an exact match with 菊.

example.english: Chrysanthemums bloom in autumn.
example.fact: 菊花 (júhuā, "chrysanthemum") is one of China's traditional "Four Gentlemen" flowers, associated with autumn.

components.note: 阝 (village) — an older semantic link to a remote, rustic place, hence 鄙's sense of "low, base."
啚 (bǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 鄙.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn bǐshì zhè zhǒng xíngwéi.
example.english: I really despise this kind of behavior.
example.fact: 鄙 usually appears in 鄙视 (bǐshì, "to despise, to look down on").

components.note: 鬼 (spirit) — 魄 relates to the soul or spirit.
白 (bái) gives a sound distantly related to pò, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He does things with great boldness.
example.fact: 魄 originally referred to the spiritual/physical soul in Chinese belief, and today survives in words like 魂魄 (húnpò, "soul") and 气魄 (qìpò, "boldness of spirit").

meanings: to wrap up or hold in a bag
etymologyHint: A man wearing a helmet, now meaning "pouch"

components.note: The character was originally a drawing of a man's head wearing a helmet with a chin strap; the shape was later borrowed to mean a hanging pouch or pocket, as the strap under the chin resembles a bag.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de qiánbāo zài kùzi dōu lǐ.
example.english: My wallet is in my pants pocket.
example.fact: 兜 today most commonly means a pocket or pouch, as in 裤兜 (kùdōu, "trouser pocket").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哄 describes a noise made by many mouths at once.
共 (gòng) gives a sound distantly related to hōng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Everyone burst out laughing after hearing it.
example.fact: With this pronunciation (hōng), 哄 describes a sudden burst of noise or laughter from a crowd, as in the idiom 哄堂大笑 (hōngtángdàxiào).

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 颖 originally named the sharp tip of a grain stalk.
匕 (bǐ) gives a sound distantly related to yǐng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This child is very bright.
example.fact: 颖 describes cleverness or sharpness of mind, as in 聪颖 (cōngyǐng, "intelligent").

components.note: 钅 (metal) — an older semantic link to money made of metal.
旁 (páng) gives a sound close to bàng, sharing the same final.

example.english: That bag cost fifty pounds.
example.fact: 镑 is used for currencies called "pound," most often 英镑 (yīngbàng, "British pound sterling").

components.note: 尸 (body) — used here as a general radical, unrelated in meaning to 屑's modern sense.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound close to xiè, sharing the same initial.

example.english: There are many paper scraps on the floor.
example.fact: 屑 refers to tiny fragments or crumbs, as in 纸屑 (zhǐxiè, "paper scraps") or 面包屑 (miànbāoxiè, "breadcrumbs").

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蚁 names a small insect.
义 (yì) gives a sound close to yǐ, differing only in tone.

example.english: The ants are carrying food.
example.fact: 蚁 is always paired with 蚂 to form 蚂蚁 (mǎyǐ, "ant").

components.note: The character was originally a drawing of a tall jar with a lid, used for holding wine or liquid — the source of 壶's meaning 'pot, kettle, jar.'

example.pinyin: Zhuō shàng yǒu yí gè cháhú.
example.english: There's a teapot on the table.
example.fact: 壶 refers to a pot or kettle with a handle and spout, as in 茶壶 (cháhú, "teapot") or 水壶 (shuǐhú, "water kettle").

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怡 describes an inner state of contentment.
台 (tái) gives a sound distantly related to yí, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 怡是一个常见的女孩名字。
example.pinyin: Yí shì yí gè chángjiàn de nǚhái míngzi.
example.english: Yi is a common girl's name.
example.fact: 怡 conveys a feeling of harmony and contentment, and is a popular character in Chinese given names, especially for girls.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渗 describes liquid seeping through.
参 (shēn) gives a sound close to shèn, sharing the same initial and rhyme.

example.pinyin: Yǔshuǐ shèntòu dào le tǔ lǐ.
example.english: Rainwater seeped into the soil.
example.fact: 渗 describes liquid slowly soaking through something, as in 渗透 (shèntòu, "to permeate, to infiltrate").

etymologyHint: Grains of hair 禾 on a person's head 几

components.note: 禾 (a grain plant) is used here to picture sparse tufts of hair remaining on a head.
几 forms the 'head' beneath — together, the picture is of a head with only a few strands left, giving 秃 its meaning 'bald.'

example.pinyin: Yéye de tóu shì tū de.
example.english: Grandpa's head is bald.
example.fact: 秃 describes baldness or bareness, whether of a head (秃头 tūtóu) or a barren mountain (秃山).

components.note: 辶 (walk) — a semantic radical common in characters used for foreign transliteration.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 迦.

example.hanzi: 释迦牟尼是佛教创始人。
example.english: Shakyamuni is the founder of Buddhism.
example.fact: 迦 has no meaning of its own — it's used purely to represent sounds in transliterated words, most famously in 释迦牟尼 (Shìjiāmóuní, "Shakyamuni," the Buddha's name).

etymologyHint: The sun 日 baking a desert 干; 干 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 日 (sun) blazes down from above.
干 here suggests dry ground — together with the sun above, the picture is of scorching heat baking the earth, giving 旱 its meaning 'drought, dry.'

example.english: There was a drought disaster this year.
example.fact: 旱 describes a lack of rain, as in 干旱 (gānhàn, "dry, arid") or 旱灾 (hànzāi, "drought").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哟 is a sound made with the mouth.
约 (yuē) gives a sound distantly related to yō, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Ouch, that hurts!
example.fact: 哟 is a spoken interjection expressing surprise or mild pain, most often heard in 哎哟 (āiyō, "ouch, oh!").

etymologyHint: One 一 voice 口 surrounded by conflict 戈

components.note: 戈 (a weapon) wraps around the character, suggesting a gathered group under arms.
一 (one) sits inside.
口 (mouth, voice) completes the picture — 'one voice' surrounded by 戈, giving 咸 its old meaning 'together, all, united.'

example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng lǎoshào xián yí.
example.english: This movie is suitable for people of all ages.
example.fact: 咸 here keeps its old meaning "all, together," preserved in the idiom 老少咸宜 (lǎoshào xiányí, "suitable for both old and young"), rather than its far more common modern sense "salty."

etymologyHint: A bird 鳥 with a strange head

components.note: The character was originally a drawing of a bird with a distinctive head or crest; this concrete picture was later completely borrowed to serve as a classical grammatical word meaning 'where, how, thereupon' — the two meanings are unrelated.

example.hanzi: 他上课的时候心不在焉。
example.pinyin: Tā shàngkè de shíhou xīn bù zài yān.
example.english: He was absent-minded during class.
example.fact: Although 焉 originally depicted a bird, it survives today mainly in classical-style idioms like 心不在焉 (xīn bù zài yān, "to be distracted, absent-minded").

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谴 is expressed through spoken or written words.
遣 (qiǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 谴.

example.pinyin: Dàjiā dōu qiǎnzé zhè zhǒng xíngwéi.
example.english: Everyone condemns this kind of behavior.
example.fact: 谴 almost always appears in 谴责 (qiǎnzé, "to condemn, to denounce").

components.note: 宀 (roof) — an older semantic link now largely faded from 宛's modern literary meaning.
夗 (yuàn) gives a sound distantly related to wǎn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The scenery here is just like a fairyland.
example.fact: 宛 is a literary word meaning "as if, seemingly," most often seen in 宛如 (wǎnrú) or 宛若 (wǎnruò).

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稻 names a grain-bearing plant.
舀 (yǎo) gives a sound distantly related to dào, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Farmers work in the rice fields.
example.fact: 稻 refers to the rice plant itself, as in 水稻 (shuǐdào, "paddy rice") — a staple crop across China.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铸 involves shaping molten metal.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound distantly related to zhù, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò zhōng shì yòng tóng zhùzào de.
example.english: This bell was cast from bronze.
example.fact: 铸 describes shaping metal by pouring it molten into a mold, as in 铸造 (zhùzào, "to cast, to forge").

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锻 originally described working metal by heat and force.
段 (duàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 锻.

example.english: I exercise every day.
example.fact: 锻 originally meant forging metal by heating and hammering, and today survives in 锻炼 (duànliàn), meaning "to exercise, to work out" — training the body like tempering metal.

meanings: used in the transliteration of Greek letters

components.note: 亻 (person) — a semantic radical common in characters used for foreign transliteration.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 伽.

example.english: She practices yoga every day.
example.fact: 伽 has no meaning of its own — it's used to transliterate foreign sounds, as in 瑜伽 (yújiā, "yoga") from Sanskrit.

components.note: 言 (speech) — an older semantic link to talking at length.
厂 (chǎng) gives a sound distantly related to zhān, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: His surname is Zhan.
example.fact: 詹 is mostly used as a surname today, and also appears in transliterations of foreign names like 詹姆斯 (Zhānmǔsī, "James").

components.note: 死 (death) — 毙 relates directly to dying.
比 (bǐ) gives a sound close to bì, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 警察击毙了那只受伤的动物。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá jībì le nà zhī shòushāng de dòngwù.
example.english: The police shot the injured animal dead.
example.fact: 毙 mostly appears in 击毙 (jībì, "to shoot dead").

meanings: (bound form) in a hazy state of mind
(bound form) to snap out of that state
used in 恍如[huang3 ru2] and 恍若[huang3 ruo4]

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 恍 describes a state of mind.
光 (guāng) gives a sound close to huǎng, sharing the same final.

example.english: He suddenly understood everything.
example.fact: 恍 usually appears in 恍然大悟 (huǎngrán dàwù), an idiom describing the moment something suddenly becomes clear.

etymologyHint: To devalue 乏 currency 贝

components.note: 贝 (shell money, i.e. currency) sits on the left.
乏 means 'lacking, deficient' — paired with currency 贝, the image is of value running short, giving 贬 its meaning 'to devalue, to demote.'

example.english: This currency has depreciated.
example.fact: 贬 describes a decrease in value or status, as in 贬值 (biǎnzhí, "to devalue") for money or 贬低 (biǎndī, "to belittle") for people.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 烛 relates to a flame.
虫 (chóng) gives a sound distantly related to zhú, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: There are candles on the birthday cake.
example.fact: 烛 always pairs with 蜡 to form 蜡烛 (làzhú, "candle").

components.note: 马 (horse) — an older semantic link to a horse startling or bolting in fright.
亥 (hài) gives the sound — an exact match with 骇.

example.english: This news is shocking.
example.fact: 骇 describes shock or fright, as in 骇人 (hàirén, "shocking, appalling") or 惊涛骇浪 (jīngtāo hàilàng, "terrifying huge waves," an idiom for danger).

etymologyHint: The heart 心 of a plant 艹; 心 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (plant) sits on top.
心, literally 'heart,' here represents the central core inside a plant stem — together giving 芯 its meaning 'pith, wick, core' (as in a lamp wick or battery core).

example.pinyin: Shǒujī lǐ yǒu yí gè xīnpiàn.
example.english: There's a chip inside the phone.
example.fact: 芯 today is best known from 芯片 (xīnpiàn, "microchip"), extending its old meaning of "core" to modern electronics.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汁 names a liquid.
十 (shí) gives a sound distantly related to zhī, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I like drinking fruit juice.
example.fact: 汁 refers to the liquid squeezed from something, most commonly in 果汁 (guǒzhī, "fruit juice").

components.note: 木 (tree) — 桓 originally named a type of tree.
亘 (gèn) gives a sound distantly related to huán, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 齐桓公是古代一位有名的君主。
example.pinyin: Qí Huán Gōng shì gǔdài yí wèi yǒumíng de jūnzhǔ.
example.english: Duke Huan of Qi was a famous ancient ruler.
example.fact: 桓 today is mostly seen in historical names, such as 齐桓公 (Qí Huán Gōng), a famous ruler from ancient China's Spring and Autumn period.

meanings: lane (usually as part of a street name)

components.note: 土 (earth) — 坊 originally named a walled quarter of a city.
方 (fāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 坊.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì jiā lǎo zuōfang.
example.english: This is an old workshop.
example.fact: 坊 refers to a small workshop or a lane/quarter in a city, as in 作坊 (zuōfang, "workshop").

components.note: 马 (horse) — 驴 names an animal related to the horse.
户 (hù) gives a sound distantly related to lǘ, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 驴是一种能干活的动物。
example.pinyin: Lǘ shì yì zhǒng néng gàn huó de dòngwù.
example.english: The donkey is an animal that can do work.
example.fact: 驴 (donkeys) have long been used in China as working animals for carrying loads and pulling carts.

etymologyHint: The wood of a dying 丂 tree 木

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) sits on the left.
丂 pictures something bent or in decline — paired with wood 木, this gives 朽 its meaning 'decayed, rotten.'

example.pinyin: Zhè kuài mùtou yǐjīng fǔxiǔ le.
example.english: This piece of wood has already rotted.
example.fact: 朽 describes decay, especially of wood, and is often seen in 不朽 (bùxiǔ, "immortal, never decaying") — describing lasting fame or work.

etymologyHint: As peaceful 立 as nature 青; 青 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 立 (to stand, stable) sits on the left.
青 (the blue-green of nature) suggests a tranquil natural scene — together giving 靖 its meaning 'peaceful, calm.'

example.pinyin: Jìng shì yí gè chángjiàn de míngzi.
example.english: Jing is a common name.
example.fact: 靖 conveys peace and stability, and is a popular character in Chinese given names and place names.

etymologyHint: An employed 用 person 亻; 用 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) sits on the left.
用 (to use) — paired with person 亻, this pictures someone being 'used,' i.e. employed, giving 佣 its meaning 'servant, commission (paid for a service).'

example.pinyin: Zhōngjiè shōu le hěn duō yōngjīn.
example.english: The agent charged a lot of commission.
example.fact: 佣 usually appears in 佣金 (yōngjīn, "commission fee"), paid to a middleman for arranging a deal.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汝 was originally the name of a river; the pronoun sense was borrowed later.
女 (nǚ) gives a sound close to rǔ, sharing the same final.

example.pinyin: Gǔwén lǐ, rǔ de yìsi shì nǐ.
example.english: In classical Chinese, 汝 means 你 (you).
example.fact: 汝 is the classical Chinese word for "you," replaced by 你 (nǐ) in modern Mandarin, but still seen in old texts and idioms.

components.note: 石 (rock) — 碌 originally described a rough, uneven stone surface.
录 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 碌.

example.english: Mom is busy every day.
example.fact: 碌 almost always appears in 忙碌 (mánglù, "busy, hectic").

components.note: 辶 (walk) — 迄 describes reaching or extending to a point.
乞 (qǐ) gives a sound close to qì, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 迄今为止,一切都很顺利。
example.pinyin: Qìjīn wéizhǐ, yíqiè dōu hěn shùnlì.
example.english: Up until now, everything has gone smoothly.
example.fact: 迄 usually appears in 迄今 (qìjīn, "up to now") or 迄今为止 (qìjīn wéizhǐ, "so far").

meanings: short name for Hebei 河北[He2 bei3]

components.note: 北 (north) — 冀 came to be associated with the northern Hebei region.
異 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to jì, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Jì shì Héběi Shěng de jiǎnchēng.
example.english: 冀 is the abbreviation for Hebei Province.
example.fact: 冀 is the official one-character abbreviation for 河北 (Héběi) province, seen on car license plates as 冀.

meanings: chaste tree or its berry (Vitex agnus-castus)
etymologyHint: A plant 艹 armed with thorns 刂

components.note: 艹 (plant) forms the top-left.
刂, pictured here as sharp thorns, combines with the plant 艹 to give 荆 its meaning 'brambles, thorny shrub.'

example.english: The road ahead is full of thorny brambles.
example.fact: 荆 refers to thorny bushes, and appears in the idiom 披荆斩棘 (pī jīng zhǎn jí, "to hack through brambles," meaning to overcome great difficulties).

etymologyHint: A bird 隹 faced with a mountain 山

components.note: 山 (mountain) sits on top.
隹 (a bird) sits below the mountain — the picture of a bird before a towering peak gave 崔 its original meaning 'high, lofty'; today it survives mainly as the surname Cui.

example.english: His surname is Cui.
example.fact: 崔 is common today as a Chinese surname, though it originally described mountains as "high, towering."

components.note: 隹 (a short-tailed bird) — 雁 names the wild goose, a migratory bird.

example.hanzi: 大雁每年都会飞往南方。
example.pinyin: Dàyàn měinián dōu huì fēiwǎng nánfāng.
example.english: Wild geese fly south every year.
example.fact: 雁 (wild geese) are famous for flying in V-shaped formations during their long seasonal migrations.

components.note: 纟 (silk) — 绅 originally named the silk sash worn by officials.
申 (shēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 绅.

example.hanzi: 他是一位很有礼貌的绅士。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi hěn yǒu lǐmào de shēnshì.
example.english: He is a very polite gentleman.
example.fact: 绅 usually appears in 绅士 (shēnshì, "gentleman"), a word borrowed to translate the English concept.

components.note: 王 (jade) — an older semantic link to precious, ornamental materials.
册 (cè) gives a sound distantly related to shān, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: There is a lot of coral on the seabed.
example.fact: 珊 always pairs with 瑚 to form 珊瑚 (shānhú, "coral").

etymologyHint: A sign posted 旁 on a tree 木; 旁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) — in old times, notices were posted on wooden boards.
旁 (beside, attached) — combined with wood, the picture is of a notice board posted up for public view, giving 榜 its meaning 'list, placard' (as in an exam results list).

example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē shàng le páihángbǎng.
example.english: This song made it onto the charts.
example.fact: 榜 refers to a publicly posted list, as in 排行榜 (páihángbǎng, "ranking chart") or historically, the list of successful exam candidates.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诵 is spoken aloud.
甬 (yǒng) gives a sound distantly related to sòng, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The students are reciting the text aloud.
example.fact: 诵 usually appears in 朗诵 (lǎngsòng, "to recite aloud") or 背诵 (bèisòng, "to recite from memory").

etymologyHint: Someone 亻 by your side 旁; 旁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) sits on the left.
旁 (side, beside) — paired with person 亻, this directly pictures being 'by someone's side,' giving 傍 its meaning 'near, close to.'

example.pinyin: Bàngwǎn de shíhou tiān hěn liáng.
example.english: In the evening it's quite cool.
example.fact: 傍 usually appears in 傍晚 (bàngwǎn, "evening, dusk"), literally meaning the time "close to" night.

components.note: 彡 (hair, decorative markings) — an older semantic link to fine ornamentation.
产 (chǎn) gives a sound distantly related to yàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 彦是一个很有文化气息的名字。
example.pinyin: Yàn shì yí gè hěn yǒu wénhuà qìxī de míngzi.
example.english: Yan is a name with a cultured feel.
example.fact: 彦 describes an accomplished, refined person and is a popular character in Chinese given names, especially for boys.

etymologyHint: Wine 酉 fit to be savored 享

components.note: 酉 (a wine jar) sits on the left.
享 (to enjoy) — paired with wine 酉, this pictures a wine worth savoring, giving 醇 its meaning 'rich, pure' (of flavor, especially alcohol).

example.pinyin: Zhè píng jiǔ wèidào hěn chún.
example.english: This wine tastes very rich and mellow.
example.fact: 醇 describes a rich, smooth flavor especially in wine, and appears in chemistry terms like 乙醇 (yǐchún, "ethanol").

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) sits on top — flutes were traditionally made of bamboo.
由, pictured here as a hollow tube, combines with bamboo ⺮ to give 笛 its meaning 'flute.'

example.english: He can play the flute.
example.fact: 笛 (dízi) is one of the oldest Chinese musical instruments, traditionally made of bamboo.

etymologyHint: A legendary beast 离 captured by a man 人

components.note: 人 (person) sits on top.
离 depicts a legendary beast — shown here beneath a person, as if captured, giving 禽 its meaning 'birds, fowl' (originally 'to capture').

example.english: Chickens are a type of poultry.
example.fact: 禽 refers to birds in general, most often in 家禽 (jiāqín, "poultry," domesticated birds like chickens and ducks).

etymologyHint: A knife 勹 cutting fragments 丿 off

components.note: 勹, here resembling a knife or wrapping motion.
丿丿 depict small fragments being cut away — together the image is of removing or forbidding something, giving 勿 its meaning 'do not, must not.'

example.english: Please do not smoke.
example.fact: 勿 is a formal way to say "don't," commonly seen on signs like 请勿吸烟 (qǐng wù xīyān, "no smoking").

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娟 describes feminine grace.
肙 (yuān) gives a sound close to juān, sharing the same final.

example.pinyin: Tā de zì xiě de hěn juānxiù.
example.english: Her handwriting is delicate and graceful.
example.fact: 娟 describes graceful beauty and is a common character in Chinese women's given names.

meanings: (fig.) to aim one's looks at; to glance at

components.note: 目 (eye) — 瞄 is an action done with the eyes.
苗 (miáo) gives the sound — an exact match with 瞄.

example.english: He aimed at the target.
example.fact: 瞄 usually appears in 瞄准 (miáozhǔn, "to aim, to take aim").

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 幢 named a cloth banner or curtain.
童 (tóng) gives a sound distantly related to chuáng, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 古代军队常用幢做旗子。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài jūnduì cháng yòng chuáng zuò qízi.
example.english: Ancient armies often used chuáng as banners.
example.fact: This character has a separate, more common modern reading zhuàng, used as a measure word for buildings, e.g. 一幢楼 (yí zhuàng lóu, "a building") — a different reading from chuáng, its meaning here as a historical banner or pennant.

etymologyHint: Bandits mugging 攴 a person 元 in his home 宀

components.note: 宀 (a roof) represents a home.
元, here representing a person, is set inside the home.
攴 (a hand wielding a weapon) strikes at the person within — together picturing bandits attacking someone in their own house, giving 寇 its meaning 'bandit, invader.'

example.hanzi: 古代山里常有寇匪出没。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài shān lǐ cháng yǒu kòufěi chūmò.
example.english: In ancient times, bandits often appeared in the mountains.
example.fact: 寇 is a literary/historical word for bandits or invaders, as in 流寇 (liúkòu, "roving bandits").

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睹 is an action done with the eyes.
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to dǔ, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ qīnyǎn mùdǔ le zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: I personally witnessed this matter.
example.fact: 睹 almost always appears in 目睹 (mùdǔ, "to witness with one's own eyes").

etymologyHint: To possess 有 wealth 贝

components.note: 贝 (shell money, wealth) sits on the left.
有 (to have) — paired with wealth 贝, this pictures someone possessing money improperly, giving 贿 its meaning 'to bribe.'

example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi huìlù bèi zhuā le.
example.english: He was caught because of bribery.
example.fact: 贿 almost always appears in 贿赂 (huìlù, "to bribe, bribery").

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踩 is an action done with the foot.
采 (cǎi) gives the sound — an exact match with 踩.

example.pinyin: Bié cǎi dào wǒ de jiǎo.
example.english: Don't step on my foot.
example.fact: 踩 is the everyday word for stepping or treading on something, as in 踩到 (cǎi dào, "to step on").

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霆 relates to a weather phenomenon.
廷 (tíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 霆.

example.english: He flew into a rage.
example.fact: 霆 always pairs with 雷 to form 雷霆 (léitíng, "thunder"), also used figuratively for a burst of anger, as in 大发雷霆 (dà fā léitíng, "to blow up in fury").

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呜 is a sound made with the mouth.
乌 (wū) gives the sound — an exact match with 呜.

example.english: She started sobbing sadly.
example.fact: 呜 is an onomatopoeic character for crying or a low mournful sound, as in 呜咽 (wūyè, "to sob") or 呜呜 (wūwū, a crying sound).

meanings: to cup one's hands in salute

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拱 originally described a hand gesture.
共 (gòng) gives a sound close to gǒng, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Gōngyuán ménkǒu yǒu yí gè gǒngmén.
example.english: There is an archway at the park entrance.
example.fact: 拱 describes an arched shape, as in 拱门 (gǒngmén, "archway"), or the traditional greeting gesture of cupping one's hands.

etymologyHint: One's own 己 woman 女

components.note: 女 (woman) sits on the left.
己 (oneself, one's own) — paired with woman 女, this pictures 'one's own woman,' i.e. a wife, giving 妃 its meaning, which later narrowed to 'imperial concubine.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì gǔdài de yí wèi wángfēi.
example.english: She was a royal consort in ancient times.
example.fact: 妃 refers to a high-ranking consort of an emperor or prince, as in 王妃 (wángfēi, "princess consort").

example.english: He despises this kind of behavior.
example.fact: 蔑 usually appears in 蔑视 (mièshì, "to despise, to look down on") or 侮蔑 (wǔmiè, "to insult").

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谕 is an instruction communicated in words.
俞 (yú) gives a sound close to yù, sharing the same final.

example.pinyin: Huángdì xià le yí dào yùzhǐ.
example.english: The emperor issued an edict.
example.fact: 谕 is a formal, historical word for an official order or instruction, as in 谕旨 (yùzhǐ, "imperial edict").

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 缚 describes tying with rope or cord.
尃 (fū) gives a sound close to fù, sharing the same initial.

example.pinyin: Guīju shùfù le tā de zìyóu.
example.english: The rules restricted his freedom.
example.fact: 缚 usually appears in 束缚 (shùfù, "to bind, to restrict"), describing both literal ropes and figurative constraints.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诡 relates to deceptive words or schemes.
危 (wēi) gives a sound distantly related to guǐ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This matter is very strange and eerie.
example.fact: 诡 describes something sly or strange, as in 诡计 (guǐjì, "cunning scheme") or 诡异 (guǐyì, "eerie, bizarre").

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 篷 was traditionally made of woven bamboo.
逢 (féng) gives a sound close to péng, sharing a related initial sound.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài shān shàng dā le zhàngpeng.
example.english: We set up a tent on the mountain.
example.fact: 篷 usually appears in 帐篷 (zhàngpeng, "tent"), traditionally covered with bamboo matting or cloth.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淹 describes being covered by water.
奄 (yǎn) gives a sound close to yān, sharing the same initial.

example.english: Floodwater submerged the village.
example.fact: 淹 describes being submerged or flooded, as in 淹没 (yānmò) or 淹死 (yānsǐ, "to drown").

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 腕 names a body part.
宛 (wǎn) gives a sound close to wàn, differing only in tone.

example.english: My wrist hurts a lot.
example.fact: 腕 refers to the wrist, most often in 手腕 (shǒuwàn), and is also used figuratively for skill, as in 铁腕 (tiěwàn, "iron-fisted").

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 煮 involves cooking with heat.
者 (zhě) gives a sound close to zhǔ, sharing the same initial.

example.english: Mom is cooking rice.
example.fact: 煮 is the everyday word for cooking something by boiling it in water, as in 煮饭 (zhǔ fàn, "to cook rice") or 煮面 (zhǔ miàn, "to boil noodles").

etymologyHint: A young 青 person 亻; 青 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) sits on the left.
青 (fresh, youthful) — paired with person 亻, this suggests someone youthful and attractive, giving 倩 its meaning 'beautiful, lovely.'

example.hanzi: 倩是一个很受欢迎的女孩名字。
example.pinyin: Qiàn shì yí gè hěn shòu huānyíng de nǚhái míngzi.
example.english: Qian is a very popular girl's name.
example.fact: 倩 describes delicate beauty and is a popular character in Chinese women's given names.

components.note: The character was originally a drawing of a soldier wearing armor marked with a distinctive pattern — giving 卒 its early meaning 'foot soldier,' which extended to 'servant' and, through the idea of a soldier's duty ending, 'at last, finally.'

example.hanzi: 象棋里最小的棋子叫卒。
example.pinyin: Xiàngqí lǐ zuì xiǎo de qízǐ jiào zú.
example.english: In Chinese chess, the smallest piece is called 卒 (a soldier).
example.fact: In Chinese chess (象棋), 卒 is the name of the pawn — the humble foot soldier, matching the character's ancient military meaning.

components.note: 力 (strength) — an older semantic link to effortful, careful work.
甚 (shèn) gives a sound distantly related to kān, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 工程师在勘察这片土地。
example.pinyin: Gōngchéngshī zài kānchá zhè piàn tǔdì.
example.english: The engineer is surveying this piece of land.
example.fact: 勘 describes careful investigation or surveying, as in 勘探 (kāntàn, "to prospect for resources") or 勘察 (kānchá, "to survey").

components.note: 香 (incense, fragrance) — 馨 originally described a pleasant, spreading fragrance.
殸 (qìng) gives a sound distantly related to xīn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: This home is warm and cozy.
example.fact: 馨 usually appears in 温馨 (wēnxīn, "warm, cozy"), describing a comforting atmosphere rather than a literal smell.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — an older semantic link to enticing someone to follow along.
豆 (dòu) gives the sound — an exact match with 逗.

example.english: This puppy is very funny.
example.fact: In modern spoken Mandarin, 逗 has taken on the casual meaning "funny, amusing," as in 你真逗 (nǐ zhēn dòu, "you're so funny").

components.note: 勹 (wrap) — an older semantic link to an enclosed area of land.
田 (tián) gives a sound close to diān, sharing the same rhyme.

example.pinyin: Běifāng huà lǐ, diànzi zhǐ cǎoyuán.
example.english: In Northern dialects, 甸子 refers to grassland.
example.fact: 甸 originally referred to the suburbs or fields around a capital city, and survives today in place names and the Northeastern dialect word 甸子 (diànzi, "grassland, pasture").

etymologyHint: Costing little 戋 money 贝; 戋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 贝 (currency, wealth) sits on the left.
戋 means 'small, little' — paired with money 贝, this pictures something costing very little, giving 贱 its meaning 'cheap, of low value.'

example.pinyin: Tā juéde zhège dōngxi hěn jiàn.
example.english: He thinks this thing is very cheap and worthless.
example.fact: 贱 today mostly carries a negative tone, describing something of low value or low social status, unlike the neutral word for "cheap," 便宜 (piányi).

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炒 involves cooking with high heat.
少 (shǎo) gives a sound distantly related to chǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: Mom is stir-frying vegetables.
example.fact: 炒 is the classic Chinese cooking technique of stir-frying quickly in a hot wok, as in 炒菜 (chǎo cài, "to stir-fry dishes").

components.note: 火 (fire) — 灿 describes brightness like a flame.
山 (shān) gives a sound distantly related to càn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The sunshine is brilliant.
example.fact: 灿 almost always appears in 灿烂 (cànlàn, "bright, splendid"), describing dazzling light or a bright future or smile.

meanings: open to the view of all

components.note: 攵 (an action radical) — an older semantic link to opening something up.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound close to chǎng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.english: This room is very spacious.
example.fact: 敞 usually appears in 宽敞 (kuānchǎng, "spacious, roomy").

meanings: as a non-simplified form sometimes used as an equivalent to

components.note: 虫 (insect) — an older semantic link to beeswax, made by insects.
昔 (xī) gives a sound distantly related to là, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The candle lit up the room.
example.fact: 蜡 refers to wax, historically linked to insects since beeswax was a major traditional source; today it's mostly seen in 蜡烛 (làzhú, "candle").

etymologyHint: A person 人 in a cell 囗

components.note: 囗 (an enclosure) surrounds the character.
人 (person) sits inside — a person trapped in an enclosure, giving 囚 its meaning 'prisoner, to confine.'

example.pinyin: Jiānyù lǐ guān zhe hěn duō qiúfàn.
example.english: Many prisoners are held in the prison.
example.fact: 囚 vividly shows its own meaning — a person 人 boxed inside an enclosure 囗 — and appears in 囚犯 (qiúfàn, "prisoner").

etymologyHint: A tree 木 bearing nuts 覀; compare 果

components.note: 覀, shown here as round nuts, sits above.
木 (tree) sits below — together giving a picture of a tree bearing nuts, hence 栗's meaning 'chestnut.'

example.english: In autumn you can eat sugar-roasted chestnuts.
example.fact: 栗子 (lìzi, "chestnuts") are a popular autumn and winter street snack in China, often sold sugar-roasted.

components.note: 辛 (bitter, suffering) — 辜 relates to wrongdoing and its consequences.
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to gū, differing only in tone.

example.english: He is innocent.
example.fact: 辜 almost always appears in 无辜 (wúgū, "innocent, not guilty").

components.note: 土 (earth) — an older semantic link to a raised base or foundation.
执 (zhí) gives a sound distantly related to diàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Yǐzi shàng yǒu yí gè diànzi.
example.english: There's a cushion on the chair.
example.fact: 垫 refers to a cushion or pad placed under something, as in 垫子 (diànzi), or figuratively "to front money" for someone, as in 垫钱 (diàn qián).

components.note: 女 (woman) — an older semantic link now largely faded from 妒's modern general meaning.
户 (hù) gives a sound distantly related to dù, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn jídù tā de chénggōng.
example.english: I am very jealous of his success.
example.fact: 妒 usually appears in 嫉妒 (jídù, "to envy, to be jealous").

etymologyHint: One who fought 斗 a ghost 鬼; 鬼 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 鬼 (ghost) forms the main body of the character.
斗 (to fight, or a ladle shape) — combined with the ghost 鬼, an old image of a heroic figure standing out from the crowd, giving 魁 its meaning 'chief, outstanding leader.'

example.pinyin: Tā zài bǐsài zhōng duókuí le.
example.english: He won first place in the competition.
example.fact: 魁 describes someone outstanding or a leader, as in 夺魁 (duókuí, "to take first place") or 罪魁祸首 (zuìkuí huòshǒu, "chief culprit," an idiom).

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谣 is spread through spoken words.
䍃 (yáo) gives the sound — an exact match with 谣.

example.pinyin: Wǎng shàng yǒu hěn duō yáoyán.
example.english: There are many rumors online.
example.fact: 谣 covers both folk songs (民谣 mínyáo) and unfounded rumors (谣言 yáoyán) — two very different meanings sharing one character.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — an older semantic link to being shut away alone indoors.
莫 (mò) gives the sound — an exact match with 寞.

example.pinyin: Yí gè rén zài jiā hěn jìmò.
example.english: Being home alone is very lonely.
example.fact: 寞 almost always appears in 寂寞 (jìmò, "lonely, lonesome").

meanings: short name for Sichuan 四川[Si4 chuan1] province

example.english: 蜀 is the ancient name for Sichuan.
example.fact: 蜀 was the name of an ancient kingdom in what is now Sichuan, and the character is still used today as Sichuan's official one-character abbreviation.

components.note: 甩 is visually the character 用 ('to use') with an added stroke pulled outward from the frame — as if something is being flung out of use, giving 甩 its meaning 'to throw, to fling, to discard.'

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shǒujī shuǎi dào le chuáng shàng.
example.english: He flung his phone onto the bed.
example.fact: 甩 describes a swinging, flinging motion, as in 甩手 (shuǎi shǒu, "to swing one's arms") or 甩掉 (shuǎi diào, "to throw off, to ditch").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涯 originally named the edge or shore of a body of water.
厓 (yá) gives the sound — an exact match with 涯.

example.pinyin: Tā de zhíyè shēngyá hěn chénggōng.
example.english: His career has been very successful.
example.fact: 涯 usually appears in 生涯 (shēngyá, "career, life journey") or the poetic phrase 天涯 (tiānyá, "the ends of the earth").

meanings: to rest one's head on (Taiwan pr. [zhen4])

components.note: 木 (wood) — 枕 originally named a wooden headrest.
冘 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to zhěn, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: I like soft pillows.
example.fact: 枕 refers to a pillow, most commonly in 枕头 (zhěntou); ancient Chinese pillows were often made of wood, ceramic, or stone rather than soft fabric.

etymologyHint: A person leaning forward to ask for help

components.note: The character was originally a drawing of a person bending forward with an outstretched hand, asking for help — the source of 丐's meaning 'beggar, to beg.'

example.pinyin: Jiē shàng yǒu yí gè qǐgài.
example.english: There is a beggar on the street.
example.fact: 丐 always pairs with 乞 to form 乞丐 (qǐgài, "beggar").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泳 describes moving through water.
永 (yǒng) gives the sound — an exact match with 泳.

example.english: I like going swimming on weekends.
example.fact: 泳 never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it's always part of 游泳 (yóuyǒng, "to swim").

meanings: one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions

components.note: 大 (big) — an older semantic link to a person striding with legs spread wide.
圭 (guī) gives a sound close to kuí, sharing the same final.

example.hanzi: 奎是一个常见的名字用字。
example.pinyin: Kuí shì yí gè chángjiàn de míngzi yòngzì.
example.english: Kui is a common character used in names.
example.fact: 奎 originally named a star constellation in traditional Chinese astronomy, and today survives mainly in personal and place names.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泌 describes a liquid being released.
必 (bì) gives a sound distantly related to mì, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: The body secretes sweat.
example.fact: 泌 almost always appears in 分泌 (fēnmì, "to secrete"), a biology term.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — 逾 describes moving past a limit.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 逾.

example.english: There will be a fine for overdue repayment.
example.fact: 逾 usually appears in 逾期 (yúqī, "overdue") in formal contexts like bills, contracts, or library books.

meanings: to sting or bite (of mosquito, bee etc)

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 叮 relates to biting or speaking.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 叮.

example.pinyin: Wénzi dīng le wǒ yì kǒu.
example.english: A mosquito bit me.
example.fact: 叮 describes both an insect's sting or bite, as in 蚊子叮 (wénzi dīng, "mosquito bite"), and repeated verbal reminders, as in 叮嘱 (dīngzhǔ, "to urge earnestly").

components.note: 黑 (black) — 黛 names a dark pigment.
代 (dài) gives the sound — an exact match with 黛.

example.hanzi: 黛是一个很有诗意的名字。
example.pinyin: Dài shì yí gè hěn yǒu shīyì de míngzi.
example.english: Dai is a very poetic name.
example.fact: 黛 originally referred to a dark blue-black pigment used to paint eyebrows, and today is best known from 黛玉 (Dàiyù), a famous character in the classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 燥 describes dryness, as if from heat.
喿 (zào) gives the sound — an exact match with 燥.

example.english: The air is very dry in winter.
example.fact: 燥 almost always appears in 干燥 (gānzào, "dry"), describing dry weather, skin, or climate.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掷 is an action done by hand.
郑 (zhèng) gives a sound distantly related to zhì, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā zhì le yí gè tóuzi.
example.english: He threw a die.
example.fact: 掷 is a more formal word for throwing, as in 投掷 (tóuzhì) or 掷骰子 (zhì tóuzi, "to roll dice").

etymologyHint: A plow 耤 is the means used to grow crops 艹

components.note: 艹 (plants, crops) sits on top.
耤 depicts plowing — together with crops 艹, this pictures the means of cultivation, extending to 藉's meanings 'to rely on, a mat, a pretext.'

example.hanzi: 朋友的关心给了她很大的慰藉。
example.pinyin: Péngyou de guānxīn gěi le tā hěn dà de wèijí.
example.english: Friends' care gave her great comfort.
example.fact: 藉 today mostly survives in 慰藉 (wèijí, "comfort, solace"), a more literary word than the everyday 安慰 (ānwèi).

components.note: 木 (tree) — 枢 originally named a wooden door hinge.
区 (qū) gives a sound distantly related to shū, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì shì jiāotōng shūniǔ.
example.english: This city is a transportation hub.
example.fact: 枢 usually appears in 枢纽 (shūniǔ, "hub, key link") or 中枢 (zhōngshū, "center, hub"), describing something central and pivotal.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 憎 describes a strong inner feeling.
曾 (zēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 憎.

example.pinyin: Tā hěn zēnghèn zhè zhǒng huǎngyán.
example.english: He deeply hates this kind of lie.
example.fact: 憎 usually appears in 憎恨 (zēnghèn, "to hate, to detest").

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — an older semantic link, since whales live in water like fish, though they are not actually fish.
京 (jīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 鲸.

example.hanzi: 鲸是世界上最大的动物。
example.pinyin: Jīng shì shìjiè shàng zuì dà de dòngwù.
example.english: Whales are the largest animals in the world.
example.fact: Although 鲸 (whales) share the "fish" component 鱼, they are actually mammals, not fish.

example.hanzi: 我们应该弘扬传统文化。
example.english: We should promote traditional culture.
example.fact: 弘 usually appears in 弘扬 (hóngyáng, "to promote, to carry forward"), especially with culture or values.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 倚 describes a person's posture.
奇 (qí) gives a sound distantly related to yǐ, having drifted apart over time.

example.english: He leaned against the wall.
example.fact: 倚 describes leaning or relying on something, as in 倚靠 (yǐkào) or the idiom 倚老卖老 (yǐ lǎo mài lǎo, "to presume upon one's age or seniority").
